subject: Career
title: The Ikigai Framework
description: A quick win: understand The Ikigai Framework.

hook.text: In Okinawa, Japan, people live to 100. They attribute their longevity to ikigai — a reason for being.

buildup.text: Ikigai sits at the intersection of what you love, what you're good at, what the world needs, and what pays.

discovery.text: Most people optimize for only one or two circles. Fulfillment requires all four to overlap.

twist.text: Finding your ikigai isn't instant. It's an iterative process of testing and reflecting over years.

climax.text: Map your four circles honestly. Where they overlap is your direction — even if imperfect.

punchline.text: Purpose isn't found. It's assembled, piece by piece.

quiz.question: What four elements make up the Ikigai framework?
options: What you love, what you're good at, what the world needs, what pays

details.summary: Ikigai is a Japanese concept that identifies purpose at the intersection of what you love, what you are good at, what the world needs, and what you can be paid for. It provides a structured lens for evaluating potential career paths.
details.whyItMatters: Without a framework, career decisions rely on gut feeling alone. Ikigai forces you to weigh passion, skill, impact, and economics simultaneously.
takeaways: Ikigai sits at the overlap of four life dimensions
Missing even one dimension creates dissatisfaction over time
The framework works iteratively as skills and markets evolve

faq.question: Is ikigai actually a traditional Japanese concept or a Western reinterpretation?
faq.answer: The Venn diagram popular in career coaching is largely a Western creation. The traditional Japanese concept of ikigai is broader and simpler, referring to the everyday joy of having a reason to get up in the morning rather than a career-planning tool.

faq.question: What should you do if none of the four circles overlap for you?
faq.answer: Start by expanding each circle through exploration. Take classes to grow skills, volunteer to discover passions, and research emerging markets. Overlap usually emerges through experimentation rather than introspection alone.
